text: Almost every machine-learning problem falls into one of two families, and the dividing line is a single question: do you have the answers? If your historical data includes the outcome you want to predict, you're doing supervised learning. If it doesn't, and you're hoping the algorithm reveals structure by itself, you're doing unsupervised learning.

In supervised learning, every training example has a label, the known answer. The model learns the mapping from features to label, then predicts labels for new rows. Regression predicts a number — the price of a house, next month's sales. Classification predicts a category — will this customer churn, which species is this flower. The label is what lets us grade the model, holding some rows back and comparing predictions with the truth.

In unsupervised learning there's no label column at all. The algorithm looks only at the features and finds structure — clustering groups similar rows together, like customer segments, and dimensionality reduction squeezes many columns into a few. Because there's no truth to compare against, the results need human interpretation.

Using scikit-learn's bundled iris dataset, 150 flowers across three species, with just petal length and width as features: training a supervised classifier that's given the actual species scores 97.8 percent accuracy on flowers it had never seen.

Running KMeans clustering on the exact same two features — but never showing it the species column — it still found three groups of nearly the same sizes, 50, 48, and 52. Comparing against the true species: species 0 was found perfectly, while species 1 and 2 overlap a little where their petals look similar.

Notice something important: the cluster numbers, 0, 1, 2, are arbitrary names. Cluster 2 happens to match species 1 here, but running again with a different seed could number them completely differently — only the actual grouping carries meaning.

Plotting both side by side makes this vivid — the left panel colored by true species, the right by discovered cluster. The colors on the right are simply cluster IDs, yet the shapes they trace closely echo the real species boundaries.

To figure out which family your own problem belongs to, ask: is there a column in my historical data that holds the answer I want to predict? Yes, and it's a number — supervised regression. Yes, and it's a category — supervised classification. No, I want to explore or segment — unsupervised.

You'll also hear about semi-supervised learning, a few labels among many unlabeled rows, self-supervised learning, labels created from the data itself, and reinforcement learning, by trial and reward. This course focuses on the two core families — Chapters 3 and 4 are supervised, Chapter 5 is unsupervised. Next up, lesson 3: the ML workflow that ties everything together.
